title: Before Monday's Bell

mood.label: Hope amid dread 🌥️
mood.summary: A 40 that genuinely pulls both ways from the same corner of the map: mediators finalise a staged Hamas disarmament roadmap that Israel has not publicly accepted, while Washington and Israel ready their heaviest strikes yet on Iran's energy grid — reportedly timed to finish before Monday's market open — over a night of ballistic missiles on Kyiv, the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record in Ituri, famine in Sudan and Europe's fourth heatwave, with a winning July on Wall Street, a photonic time crystal and a retinal implant that gave people back their reading holding the other column up.

style.genre: sax-led afro-highlife dub / hand-percussion groove — a VCSL balafon tracing a circling D mixolydian topline over a loose RolandCompurhythm1000 kit with darbuka, cajon, shaker and agogo hand percussion, a saxophone answering low and lyrical in the gaps, an 8-inch drawbar organ holding a I–bVII–IV–vi pad, tubular bells tolling sparse and far off for the dread, a plucked acoustic bass walking the roots under a soft sine sub; mixolydian's major third carrying the day's real hope while the lowered seventh (natural C over the D root) refuses to let it resolve — a peace roadmap and a bombing run out of the same doorway, and deliberately nothing from the piano/harp/flute/clean-guitar run of the last week

lines: Four flags signed a roadmap for the guns to go in stages,
a committee with a clipboard writing rifles onto pages —
three hundred days of handing over, if the ink still holds,
and nobody in Tel Aviv has said out loud they're sold.
So it's forty on the meter — that's hope laid over dread,
a roadmap through one doorway and a bomb run through the next;
they'll have it done by Monday so the market never sees,
and one thin strip of water holds the best and worst of these.
A missile opened August over Kyiv before the light,
three gone, and boys of thirteen and of seventeen inside it;
in Ituri the fever runs the fastest ever known,
and twenty-four million in Sudan are queuing for a bowl.
But someone in a clinic read a letter chart today —
a grain of rice behind the eye that gave the words away.
